Section 2.0 exists as a heading here but did not return substantive text, so I’ll avoid adding details from it that I cannot verify.## NC Medicaid O&P policy: items specifically **not covered** and general coverage criteria

Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, Orthotics & Prosthetics**, the following are specifically **not covered**:

- Devices for the beneficiary’s **comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- Devices kept **as backup** or **duplicates** for use at different locations
- Devices and supplies for **residents of nursing facilities**
- Devices or supplies **covered by another agency**
- Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries **receiving hospice care**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.2.1)

There are also broader noncoverage rules. NC Medicaid does **not** cover the item or service if:

- the beneficiary does not meet the **eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0,
- the beneficiary does not meet the **coverage criteria** in Section 3.0,
- the item/service **duplicates** another provider’s item/service, or
- the item/service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.1)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

For coverage, the policy requires that the procedure, product, or service be:

- **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not more than the beneficiary needs**;
- able to be **safely furnished**, with **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
- furnished in a way **not primarily intended for convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.1)

For orthotic/prosthetic items specifically, Medicaid coverage also requires that they:

- be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**;
- be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level, and be appropriate for use in a **noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place;
- be supported by a **face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician within **6 months** before initiation; and
- have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering clinician  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

The policy further says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**.
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary as a **replacement for all or part of the function** of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part, and the beneficiary must need the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**.
- Orthotic and prosthetic devices must also be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the treatment plan,
  - **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms, and
  - of **high quality**, with replacement parts **available and obtainable**  
  ([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1)

## Bottom line

The policy does **not** list brand-by-brand DME items as excluded in this section; instead, it excludes the categories above, such as convenience items, backup/duplicate items, nursing-facility resident items, items covered by another agency, and hospice-related equipment/supplies. Coverage generally depends on **medical necessity, non-convenience use, appropriateness, safety, cost-effectiveness, proper ordering, and required clinical documentation**.  
([Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), §§ 3.1, 3.2.1, 4.1, 4.2.1)

Continued services require:

### First, at least one of these:
- the desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- the beneficiary’s gains are **tenuous**. [8C § 3.2.1.2, Continued Service Criteria](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

- the beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, but **additional goals are indicated** and supported by documented symptoms; or
- the beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals** and the documentation supports continuing treatment. [8C § 3.2.1.2, Continued Service Criteria](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when:

- the beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- the beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wants the services**; or
- the beneficiary has **not improved despite modifications to the treatment plan** and needs a **more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards. Policy 8C also says outpatient behavioral health is not covered in certain situations, including when:

- treatment is **sleep therapy for psychiatric disorders**;
- services are not provided **in person or in accordance with Attachment A**;
- the beneficiary has a **medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue** that would not benefit from outpatient treatment services;
- treatment does **not address the symptoms of the diagnosis**; or
- Section 5.0 requirements and limitations are not followed. [8C § 4.2.1.1, Outpatient Behavioral Health](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## EPSDT effect on outpatient therapy coverage

For outpatient specialized therapies under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, the **EPSDT special provision** means a Medicaid beneficiary **under age 21** may receive services **beyond ordinary policy limitations** when the service is otherwise coverable under Medicaid and is needed under EPSDT standards. The policy’s EPSDT subsection expressly cites **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) [Social Security Act § 1905(r)]** and indicates that EPSDT does **not** require coverage of services that are:

- **unsafe**
- **ineffective**
- **experimental or investigational**
- **not medical in nature**
- **not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1, effective 2025-02-01)

In practical terms, that means EPSDT can operate as an **exception to policy limitations** for beneficiaries under 21, but it is **not an automatic override of all requirements**.

A key example in 10A is that the visit cap section is written specifically for **“Beneficiaries 21 Years of Age and Older,”** which supports the conclusion that ordinary adult visit limits are treated differently from EPSDT-eligible children. ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 5.3, effective 2025-02-01)

## Prior approval still applies under EPSDT

Even for beneficiaries under 21, EPSDT does **not eliminate prior approval requirements**. Policy 10A says:

> “If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.”  
([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), subsection “EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements,” effective 2025-02-01)

So, for a child or youth under 21 seeking outpatient therapy, EPSDT may support coverage beyond a standard limitation, **but the provider still must obtain prior approval when 10A requires it**.

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Policy 10A’s **Ordering Practitioners** section lists the practitioners who may order covered services:

- **Medical Doctor (MD)**
- **Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)**
- **Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)**
- **Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)**
- **Physician Assistant (PA)**
- **Nurse Practitioner (NP)**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2, effective 2025-02-01)

For treatment services, 10A also requires that:

- a **verbal or written order** be obtained **before services start**
- verbal orders must be documented and **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**
- verbal orders are valid for **up to six months** from the documented receipt date
- written orders are valid for **up to six months** from the physician’s signature date
- **backdating is not allowed**  
  ([Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), treatment-service requirements section, effective 2025-02-01)

## Bottom line

For beneficiaries **under 21**:

- **EPSDT can expand access** to outpatient therapy services beyond normal policy limits when medically necessary under EPSDT.
- But EPSDT **does not waive prior approval** requirements.
- Therapy must still be supported by an order from an authorized ordering practitioner under **§ 3.1.2**, and treatment-order documentation rules still apply.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the congregate-settings PCS policy and checked amendments; the tool reports no amendments and identifies Policy 3L-1 as the current authoritative document. I also pulled the coverage and eligibility sections. Next I’ll answer whether assisted living residents can get PCS and note the conditions the policy requires.## Short answer

**Yes—NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in assisted living-type settings, but only if they meet the policy’s eligibility criteria.**

The controlling policy for facility-based PCS is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings**, which the amendment check identified as the current authoritative document, with no amendments returned. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What settings are included

NC Medicaid says PCS in congregate settings is available for a beneficiary who resides in:

- a **congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)**,
- a **combination home**, or
- certain licensed **group homes**.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

If by “assisted living facility” you mean an **adult care home/assisted living-type congregate facility**, this policy indicates PCS can be covered there.

## Main conditions for coverage

The beneficiary must have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing unmet needs and must meet the ADL threshold. Specifically, the policy requires unmet need for at least:

- **3 of 5 qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
- **2 ADLs**, with **1 requiring extensive assistance**, or
- **2 ADLs**, with **1 requiring full dependence-level assistance**.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The policy also says, among other things, that:

- the setting must be safe and inspected,
- **no other third-party payer** can be responsible for PCS,
- no family/household/informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services at those times,
- the services must be directly linked to the documented condition causing the functional limitations,
- the beneficiary must be under the ongoing direct care of a physician, and
- the beneficiary must be medically stable and not require continuous nursing-level monitoring or supervision.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What PCS includes

The policy says Medicaid covers PCS such as:

- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs,
- related cueing/prompting/guiding when part of hands-on ADL help,
- medication assistance tied to the documented condition,
- help with adaptive or assistive devices,
- help using durable medical equipment, and
- certain special assistance and delegated medical monitoring tasks.  
  [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

**Yes, NC Medicaid may cover PCS for a beneficiary living in an assisted living/adult care home-type facility, but coverage is not automatic.** The person must live in a qualifying congregate setting and meet the medical and functional eligibility standards in Policy 3L-1. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Next I’ll pull the full CAP/DA section and the key federal sections, then check amendments for the NC CAP/DA policy before answering.## Federal authority for NC’s CAP/DA waiver

NC’s CAP/DA waiver is grounded in **section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**. NC’s own CAP/DA policy states that section 1915(c) authorizes the Secretary of Health and Human Services to waive certain Medicaid requirements so a state may offer home- and community-based services (HCBS) to state-specified target groups who meet a **nursing facility level of care**. The same CAP/DA policy also points to **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G** as the governing federal waiver regulations. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR 441.301**, a state’s waiver request must include:

- the **assurances** required by **42 CFR 441.302** and the **supporting documentation** required by **42 CFR 441.303**;
- where applicable, requests to waive Medicaid requirements such as **statewideness**, **comparability**, or certain **income/resource rules**;
- whether the state will refuse HCBS when it reasonably expects the HCBS cost to exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care;
- that services will be provided under a **written person-centered service plan**;
- that services will be furnished only to people who, absent waiver services, would require the covered institutional level of care; and
- descriptions of the target group, service definitions, and plan-of-care development. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

More specifically, the state must provide CMS with enough information to support the required assurances. Under **42 CFR 441.302** and **441.303**, that means demonstrating at least the following:

### 1. Required assurances
NC’s CAP/DA policy summarizes the waiver assurances as:

- **Level of Care**
- **Administrative Authority**
- **Qualified Providers**
- **Services Plan**
- **Health and Welfare**
- **Financial Accountability**  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The federal regulation requires satisfactory assurances on those subjects before CMS will grant or continue the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 2. Health and welfare safeguards
The state must show safeguards to protect beneficiaries’ health and welfare, including:

- adequate provider standards;
- compliance with any state licensure/certification requirements;
- compliance of covered facilities with applicable standards; and
- HCBS being provided in **home and community-based settings**.  
  Current federal rules also require an **incident management system** that identifies, reports, investigates, resolves, tracks, and trends critical incidents. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 3. Financial accountability
The state must demonstrate financial accountability for waiver funds and describe the records and information it will maintain to support that accountability. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 4. Level-of-care evaluation and reevaluation
The state must describe its plan for:

- initial evaluations and periodic reevaluations;
- who performs them and how;
- the evaluation form used;
- how documentation will be maintained; and
- how reevaluations will occur at regular intervals.  
  [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 5. Freedom of choice / feasible alternatives
The state must explain how it will:

- inform eligible individuals about feasible alternatives under the waiver; and
- allow them to choose either **institutional services** or **home- and community-based services**.  
  [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 6. Cost neutrality / cost-effectiveness showing
A key demonstration is that waiver costs will not exceed institutional costs. Under **42 CFR 441.303(f)**, the state must provide an explanation, with supporting documentation satisfactory to CMS, of how it estimated average per capita expenditures, and the estimate for waiver services plus other Medicaid services for waiver participants must be **less than or equal to** what Medicaid would have spent without the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 7. Number served / waiver cap
The state must state the number of **unduplicated beneficiaries** it intends to serve each year. That number becomes a limit on waiver size unless CMS approves an increase by amendment. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

### 8. Person-centered planning and setting compliance
The waiver request must show that services are delivered through a **person-centered planning process** and **person-centered service plan**, and that settings meet HCBS setting requirements. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## Short answer

The federal statutory authority is **Social Security Act § 1915(c)**, implemented through **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. In its waiver application, the state must give CMS the required **assurances** and **supporting documentation** showing, at minimum, that:

- beneficiaries meet the required **institutional level of care**;
- the state has proper **administrative authority** and **qualified providers**;
- services are delivered under **person-centered service plans** in compliant HCBS settings;
- beneficiary **health and welfare** will be protected;
- waiver funds will be used with **financial accountability**; and
- the waiver is **cost-neutral/cost-effective** compared with institutional care.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?

The NC policy’s “Terminally Ill” heading did not return body text, so I’m relying on the certification provisions and the federal definition text they implement, which explicitly states the 6-month prognosis standard.## NC Medicaid hospice: meaning of “terminally ill” and required certification

For **NC Medicaid hospice eligibility**, the operative standard is that the person has a **prognosis of life expectancy of 6 months or less if the terminal illness runs its normal course**. NC Medicaid’s hospice policy uses that standard through its certification rules, and the federal hospice regulation states it expressly. See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Hospice Services** (effective **Mar. 15, 2024**) and **42 CFR 418.22(b)(1)**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment); [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)

### Required certification
NC Medicaid requires a **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim**; if it cannot be obtained within **2 calendar days after the period begins**, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those 2 days and the **written certification** must still be obtained before billing. **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D § 5.4.1**; **42 CFR 418.22(a)**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment); [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)

### Who must certify
For the **initial 90-day period**, NC Medicaid requires written certification from:

- **the hospice medical director** or **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; **and**
- **the individual’s attending physician**, **if** the individual has an attending physician.

For **subsequent periods**, only the **hospice medical director** or **physician member of the IDG** must certify. **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D § 5.4.3**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)

### What the certification must contain
The certification/recertification must include:

- a **brief narrative** synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s **attestation** that the narrative was composed after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- the **benefit period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying physician’s **signature and date**.

For the **third and later benefit-period recertifications**, the narrative must also explain why the **face-to-face clinical findings** support a life expectancy of **6 months or less**. **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D, Attachment B, “Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”**; **42 CFR 418.22(b)(3)-(5)**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment); [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)

### Face-to-face requirement
Beginning with the **3rd benefit period recertification** and each one after that, a **hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner** must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary **before**, but **no more than 30 calendar days before**, that recertification, to gather clinical findings supporting continued hospice eligibility. **Clinical Coverage Policy 3D § 5.4.1**; **42 CFR 418.22(a)(4)**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment); [42 CFR Part 418](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-418)

## Bottom line
In practice, NC Medicaid hospice treats **“terminally ill”** as meaning the beneficiary is certified, based on clinical judgment and supporting documentation, as having a **life expectancy of 6 months or less if the illness follows its normal course**. Eligibility requires the **required physician certification(s)** for the relevant benefit period, with the specified narrative, signatures, dates, and later recertification face-to-face documentation.

Next I’m going to pull the federal remittance/reporting provisions directly from 42 CFR Part 438 and check amendments on the NC SPA before answering.## Short answer

Under federal Medicaid managed care law, a state that **requires a minimum medical loss ratio (MLR)** must set that minimum at **no less than 85%**. Federal rules also require the state to ensure, through its managed care contracts, that each MCO/PIHP/PAHP **calculates and reports** its MLR. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

North Carolina’s implementation evidence I could verify in the retrieved NC materials is that the state:
- assures its rates are designed to **reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio**, and
- recognizes the federal remittance/reporting framework if a plan owes money for failing the state’s minimum MLR. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### Minimum MLR
42 C.F.R. § 438.8(c) says:

- If a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its Medicaid managed care plans, **that minimum must be equal to or higher than 85 percent**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### Contract/reporting requirement
The same section also says:

- The state must ensure, **through its contracts**, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR in accordance with the regulation. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### State oversight and remittances
Federal oversight rules further require:

- The state must annually submit to CMS a summary of each plan’s MLR report, including the numerator, denominator, MLR percentage, member months, and any remittances owed.  
- If the state requires remittances when a plan fails the minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share and submit a separate methodology report. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## How NC implements it

Based on the NC document I was able to retrieve, North Carolina implements the requirement at least by incorporating the federal MLR framework into its managed care financing assurances:

- NC states that its rates are designed to **reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio**.  
- NC also states that if a remittance is owed by an MCO/PIHP/PAHP for not meeting the minimum MLR required by the state, NC will:
  - reimburse CMS for the federal share, and
  - submit a separate report describing the state/federal share methodology with the annual report to CMS. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal baseline:** minimum MLR, if imposed by the state, must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)  
- **NC implementation I could verify:** NC aligns with that framework by designing rates to reasonably achieve MLR and by using the federal remittance/reporting structure. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)
